title: Triangles Lab
text:
angles; similarity preserves angles and scales every length by one factor.

How to work it

Use SSS, SAS, ASA, or AAS for congruence, and AA or proportional sides for similarity. Centers arise from intersecting special lines: medians, perpendicular bisectors, or altitudes.

Watch for

SSA does not always determine a unique triangle; it can produce two configurations.

Three worked examples

Use the lab controls to test these relationships.

1
Roof truss

Sides 3,4,5 make a right triangle because 3²+4²=5².

Area is 3·4/2=6 square units.
2
Scale model

A 2-3-4 triangle enlarged by factor 3 becomes 6-9-12.

Perimeter triples while area grows ninefold.
3
Centroid

Vertices (0,0),(6,0),(0,3).

Median intersection is ((0+6+0)/3,(0+0+3)/3)=(2,1).
Test it in the live lab

Use transformations to move one triangle onto the other.

Why does SSS guarantee triangle congruence?

Core idea

On the unit circle, the point at angle θ is (cosθ,sinθ). The signs come from the quadrant, and reference angles let one reuse first-quadrant exact values.

How to work it

Reduce an angle modulo 360° or 2π, find its reference angle, apply quadrant signs, and read coordinates. Use tanθ=sinθ/cosθ where defined.

Watch for

Tangent is undefined at 90° and 270° because cosθ=0.

Three worked examples

Use the lab controls to test these relationships.

1
Reference angle

θ=150° has reference angle 30°.

(cosθ,sinθ)=(-√3/2,1/2).
2
Full rotation

450° is coterminal with 90°.

The terminal point is (0,1).
3
Radians

θ=5π/4.

The point is (-√2/2,-√2/2), in quadrant III.

title: Population Growth Lab
text:
wth adds carrying capacity K. Harvesting subtracts a removal term, and age-structured models replace one count with linked cohorts.

How to work it

State births, deaths, resource limit, and intervention rates, then locate equilibria and test sensitivity to parameters.

Watch for

A carrying capacity estimated in one environment may change with climate or resource use.

Three worked examples

Use the lab controls to test these relationships.

Exponential

P₀=100,r=0.2/year.

After 5 years P≈272 in the constant-rate model.
2
Logistic

K=1000,P₀=100,r=0.2/year.

P(5)=1000/(1+9e^(-1))≈232.
3
Harvest

P′=0.2P(1-P/1000)−30.

Equilibria solve 0.2P(1-P/1000)=30, and excessive harvest can remove positive equilibrium.

title: Modular Arithmetic Lab
text:
thmetic: learn and explore
Current lab mode: Clock Arithmetic
Theory & examples
In Simple words
Formulas
Real-time examples
Try these
Core idea

Congruence a≡b (mod n) means n divides a−b. Residues wrap around a finite clock; a has an inverse mod n exactly when gcd(a,n)=1.

How to work it

Reduce residues, use the Euclidean algorithm for inverses, and solve linear congruences only after checking gcd(a,n) divides b.

Watch for

Division modulo n is not ordinary division; it requires a modular inverse.

Three worked examples

Use the lab controls to test these relationships.

1
Clock

17 hours after 9 on a 12-hour clock.

9+17≡2 (mod 12).
2
Inverse

Solve 3x≡1 (mod 7).

x≡5 because 3·5=15≡1.
3
No solution

Solve 4x≡3 (mod 6).

gcd(4,6)=2 does not divide 3, so there is no residue solution.
Test it in the live lab

Solve 5x≡10 (mod 12).

Inverses exist when gcd(a,n)=1.

title: Confidence Intervals Lab
text:

How to work it

Choose the estimand and sampling model, compute a standard error, choose a critical value, and interpret the interval as a plausible parameter range.

Watch for

A fixed 95% interval does not assign 95% probability to the fixed population parameter in the usual frequentist interpretation.

p̂=0.60, SE≈0.049, approximate 95% margin ≈0.096.

About 95 should contain μ on average, but any run may differ.

title: Euler
text:
dvances y′=f(x,y) by y_(n+1)=y_n+h f(x_n,y_n). It follows the starting tangent for a whole step, so curvature creates truncation error.

How to work it

Evaluate the slope at the current point, multiply by step h, update x and y, and repeat. Halving h generally reduces first-order global error by about a factor of two.

Watch for

A small step does not guarantee stability for every equation; stiff decay can make explicit Euler oscillate or blow up.

Three worked examples

Use the lab controls to test these relationships.

1
Growth

y′=y, y(0)=1, h=0.1.

First step y₁=1.1; exact e^0.1≈1.1052.
2
Cooling

T′=-0.2(T-20), T₀=80, h=1.

Slope is -12 °C/min; Euler predicts T₁=68 °C.
3
Stability

y′=-10y, h=0.3.

Update factor 1-10h=-2, so numerical values alternate and grow despite exact decay.
Test it in the live lab
